sections.structure: The List view — the keyboard- and screen-reader-accessible version of the map.
sections.templates: Names and descriptions of the starting-point maps in the Templates dialog.
sections.templateNodes: The box labels inside each template. Everyday clinical phrasing, not technical terms — say it the way a clinician in your language would.
sections.templateNote: Appended to a template description when it is loaded.
sections.exportDialog: The Export dialog. File format names — keep JSON, CSV, PNG, SVG, PDF as they are.
sections.clearDialog: The confirmation dialog for clearing the whole map.
sections.kernel: The Treatment kernels dialog (a feature still in development).
sections.help: The Help dialog. The most-read text in the tool.
sections.about: The About dialog: credits, grounding in the literature, and the privacy statement.
sections.error: Shown only when the drawing canvas fails to start.
sections.toast: Brief messages that appear at the bottom of the screen and fade after a few seconds.
sections.a11y: Screen-reader labels. Never visible on screen, but read aloud.

entries.english:
Use the Event / context button and add the situation this is about: what happened, where, with whom. It gets a rounded box, because it is not something the person is doing.

Starting here is not a formality. In a functional assessment the same thought or action means different things in different situations, so the context is what makes everything after it interpretable.
entries.section: The step-by-step guided build panel. Long-form teaching text.

entries.english: Add an event or context box to begin.
entries.section: The step-by-step guided build panel. Long-form teaching text.

entries.english: 2. Add the response and what follows
entries.section: The step-by-step guided build panel. Long-form teaching text.

entries.english:
Now add what happens inside (a thought, feeling or urge) and what the person does or what results. Connect them in order, from the context onwards.

That is the three-term contingency, the unit a functional assessment is built from. Everything else grows out of it.
entries.section: The step-by-step guided build panel. Long-form teaching text.

entries.english: Add two more boxes: the internal response, then what happens.
entries.section: The step-by-step guided build panel. Long-form teaching text.

entries.english: Now connect them: context → internal response → what happens.
entries.section: The step-by-step guided build panel. Long-form teaching text.
The step-by-step guided build panel. Long-form teaching text.

entries.english:
Look at the end of your chain and ask: does that feed back into anything earlier? Poor sleep causes worry, but worry also causes poor sleep.

Feedback is usually the answer to why a problem persists long after whatever started it has gone.
entries.section: The step-by-step guided build panel. Long-form teaching text.

entries.english: Nothing loops back yet. Does the consequence feed anything earlier?
entries.section: The step-by-step guided build panel. Long-form teaching text.
The step-by-step guided build panel. Long-form teaching text.

entries.english:
What else is caught up in this? Add a node for anything affected by the consequence that also feeds back into the response.

Amplifiers matter here. Fatigue is not just another problem, it makes everything else feel more threatening.
entries.section: The step-by-step guided build panel. Long-form teaching text.

entries.english: Add at least one more element.
entries.section: The step-by-step guided build panel. Long-form teaching text.
The step-by-step guided build panel. Long-form teaching text.

entries.english:
Not everything makes things worse. Add something that reduces one of these problems, draw it as a decreasing link, and mark that link as Helping.

This is often the part people skip, and it is where the intervention usually lives.
entries.section: The step-by-step guided build panel. Long-form teaching text.

entries.english: Add something that reduces one of these, drawn as a decreasing link.
entries.section: The step-by-step guided build panel. Long-form teaching text.

entries.english: Mark that link as Helping, so the map shows what is working.
entries.section: The step-by-step guided build panel. Long-form teaching text.

entries.english: 6. Map what gets in the way
entries.section: The step-by-step guided build panel. Long-form teaching text.

entries.english:
Now the hard part. What stops the helpful thing from happening?

This is why "just exercise more" lands so badly. The person already knows it would help. Something in the system is suppressing it, and until that is visible the advice has nowhere to go.
entries.section: The step-by-step guided build panel. Long-form teaching text.

entries.english: Add a link that suppresses the thing that helps.
entries.section: The step-by-step guided build panel. Long-form teaching text.

entries.english: Centrality, loops and leverage describe the map that was drawn, not the person. They assume influence is linear and immediate, which it is not. They are a structured way to interrogate your own thinking, and they are worth exactly as much as the ratings they were built from.

entries.english: A free, open-source tool for mapping process-based networks: the functional relationships between the processes that maintain psychological suffering and wellbeing.
entries.section: The About dialog: credits, grounding in the literature, and the privacy statement.
The About dialog: credits, grounding in the literature, and the privacy statement.

entries.english: The categories and the way this tool thinks about processes come from the Extended Evolutionary Meta-Model set out in the process-based therapy work of **Steven C. Hayes and Stefan G. Hofmann**: affect, cognition, attention, self, motivation and overt behaviour, situated in biophysiological and sociocultural levels, and always read in context.
